summary: Documents the composition, selection, roles and organization of the Internet Architecture Board. It replaces RFC 1601. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2850 sets out who serves on the Internet Architecture Board and what the board is responsible for. It also explains how the board makes decisions and shares its work.

subtitle: The charter that defines the IAB's membership, responsibilities and decision-making process.

tldr.problem: The Internet Architecture Board needed a written charter defining its membership, responsibilities and organization.
tldr.mechanism: The charter describes the board's thirteen full members, liaison roles, work on Internet architecture and standards, and rules for decisions and meetings.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2850 replaced RFC 1601 and is a Best Current Practice. It has since been updated by RFC 9283.

sections.title: IAB Membership
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) has thirteen full members: the IETF chair and twelve sitting members. The IETF chair also chairs the IESG, but does not take part in IAB actions on approving IESG members or hearing appeals of IESG decisions.

Members serve as individuals, not as representatives of their employers or other organizations. Normally, six sitting members are appointed each year for two-year terms. Ex-officio and liaison members may join discussions but do not take part in official decisions unless an ex-officio role is held by a full member.
sections.plainLanguage: The board has thirteen full members, including the IETF chair. Members serve as individuals, while liaison and ex-officio participants can join discussions but usually do not vote.

sections.title: The IAB's Responsibilities
sections.content:
The IAB serves as a committee of the IETF and as an advisory body to the Internet Society. It consents to some, all or none of the candidates proposed for vacant IESG seats and the IETF chair. It oversees Internet architecture and the standards process, and hears appeals about improper execution of that process.

The IAB approves the organization that acts as RFC Editor and its general policy, as well as the organization that acts as IANA. It advises the Internet Society on technical and related matters and represents IETF and Internet Society interests in technical relationships with other organizations.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB advises on Internet architecture, oversees the standards process and considers appeals about that process. It also approves the organizations responsible for the RFC series and IANA.

sections.title: Architectural Oversight
sections.content:
The IAB plans for long-term Internet issues and coordinates across areas of IETF work. It watches emerging activities and proposed working groups. When the IESG sends a preliminary charter for a new working group, the IAB reviews it for architectural consistency and gives feedback.

The IAB sponsors and organizes the Internet Research Task Force and reviews proposed research groups. It may hold workshops to examine architectural issues and publish reports with advice for the IETF community and IESG. It may also convene independent technical experts to address technical disputes.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB reviews proposed work to see how it fits the Internet's architecture. It can also organize research groups, workshops and expert reviews of technical disputes.

sections.title: Leadership and Organization
sections.content:
The full members select an IAB chair for a one-year term, with no limit on renewal. The chair manages the board's activities and meetings. Two-thirds of the members may remove the chair. The chair may appoint an honorary Executive Director for a renewable one-year term to handle internal operations such as meetings and reports.

The IAB appoints the IRTF chair for a renewable two-year term and may remove that chair. The IAB chair and another full member serve as liaisons to the IESG. The IESG also appoints a liaison to the IAB.
sections.plainLanguage: The board selects its chair each year and can remove that chair by a two-thirds vote. The board also appoints the IRTF chair and maintains liaison roles with the IESG.

sections.title: Decisions and Public Work
sections.content:
The IAB tries to reach unanimous decisions. If it cannot, the chair may use informal polls to find consensus. The board may act when at least seven full members concur and there are no more than two dissents. It may make decisions in meetings, by teleconference or through Internet communication.

The IAB publishes meeting minutes online, holds an open meeting at every IETF meeting and publishes findings as RFCs, Internet-Drafts or messages to the IETF mailing list. Personnel topics, and sometimes legal or financial topics, may remain confidential.
sections.plainLanguage: The board aims for unanimous agreement. If that fails, it can act when at least seven members agree and no more than two dissent; meeting minutes and findings are generally public.

sections.title: Security and Changes from RFC 1601
sections.content: RFC 2850 says that it raises no known security threats. It replaces RFC 1601, removing material that is covered in BCP 8, BCP 9 and BCP 10. It also describes decision-making when unanimity is not possible, openness and confidentiality, and liaison seats for the Internet Society and IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC reports no known security threats. It replaced RFC 1601 and added clearer rules for decisions, public work and liaison roles.
